query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy protective coatings sliding in oxygen‐containing environments, an optimum dynamic grain‐refinement process leads to the rapid formation and stabilization of a continuous, crack‐resistant oxide (glaze) layer that concurrently lubricates the interface and impedes plastic deformation. In other words, when the near-surface structure is refined into a nano- to ultrafine-grained state (but not so extreme as to induce complete inverse Hall-Petch softening), the enhanced density of grain boundaries promotes a more uniform and mechanically robust tribo-oxidation film. This dual process produces lower friction and wear rates compared to coatings with coarse grain structure under the same wear conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy protective coating (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi or similar HEA) deposited with an initially relatively coarse microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal/mechanical pre-treatment to produce a graded reduction in grain size (targeting an ultrafine range of roughly tens-of-nanometers to ~100 nm) in the near-surface region of the coating versus a baseline coarse-grained state.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests under ambient (oxygen-containing) conditions at varied loads and sliding speeds; parallel tests in inert (e.g., UHV) environments can serve as a control to isolate the role of oxide formation.
generation.structural_mediator: The near-surface grain size and the continuity (and crack resistance) of the dynamically formed oxide (glaze) layer.
generation.mechanism: Dynamic grain refinement under high strain increases grain boundary density, which accelerates tribo-oxidation. The resulting oxide film, when continuous and less prone to cracking (thanks to the fine grain structure’s high surface strength), acts as a lubricious barrier that shields the underlying metal. In contrast, a coarse-grained surface forms a less robust, more crack-prone oxide film leading to higher friction and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under ambient sliding conditions, coatings pre-treated to exhibit an ultrafine near-surface grain structure will show a lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate due to the rapid formation of a stable, protective glaze layer. Conversely, coatings with coarse grains will exhibit more brittle, cracked oxides and thus higher friction and wear. In inert environments where oxidation is suppressed, the benefits of the stable oxide layer disappear and inverse Hall-Petch softening may instead reduce friction by a different mechanism.
generation.baseline: The untreated or as-deposited coarse-grained HEA coating, which under identical ambient sliding conditions produces a less continuous and more fractured oxide layer, leading to higher wear rates and friction.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold under conditions where oxygen is available (room temperature to moderate/high temperature in air) and for coatings whose near-surface grain sizes can be controllably refined to an optimum range (approximately 50–100 nm). It may not apply in inert atmospheres where oxidation is minimal, or if excessive grain refinement induces complete softening.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis is built by combining findings from studies on grain size effects and tribological behavior (e.g., PMC9960858::web::000 and PMC7311485::web::001) with results on the role of tribo-oxidation and protective glaze formation (e.g., PMC10241162::web::003 and related sections). The novelty lies in proposing that a controlled level of dynamic grain refinement can be tuned to promote a stable oxide layer under ambient conditions—an interplay that reconciles conflicting results observed in oxidizing versus inert environments. Uncertainty remains in the precise grain size window and the oxide layer’s mechanical resilience under variable loads.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings with otherwise identical compositions: one with a coarse-grained near-surface structure (baseline) and another with a controlled ultrafine-grained surface produced via targeted pre-treatment. Conduct identical sliding wear tests in ambient air at several loads and speeds. Use high-resolution microscopy and surface analysis (SEM, TEM, and EDS) to assess oxide film continuity and crack formation, and measure friction coefficients and wear rates.
measurements: Quantitative grain size distribution in the near-surface region (e.g., via TEM or EBSD)
Morphology and continuity of the oxide (glaze) layer
Coefficient of friction during steady-state sliding
Wear rate (material loss per unit sliding distance and load)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultrafine-grained coatings do not show a statistically significant lower friction coefficient and wear rate—along with evidence of a more continuous and crack-resistant oxide layer—compared to the coarse-grained coatings under ambient conditions, then the hypothesis that dynamic grain refinement enhances wear resistance via oxide stabilization is falsified.

Since their discovery in 2004,, high entropy alloys (HEAs) have been extensively investigated and shown to exhibit remarkable thermomechanical properties,. Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Recent work has also shown that these alloys are ideally suited for processing using laser-based additive manufacturing techniques, as they exhibit high phase stability and derive much of their strength from thermal history-insensitive mechanisms like solution strengthening. While recent publications have presented experimental evidence of low friction or high wear resistance (but typically not both) with HEAs, they were performed in environments where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide surface films was prevalent. These phenomena can greatly impact strength and deformation/wear resistance. AbstractThe effect and mechanism of grain sizes on the tribological behavior of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (HEA) were studied by friction experiments and wear morphology analysis. Under normal low load and low sliding speed, the primary wear mechanism of the HEA samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the samples are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. The oxide layer formed under the action of friction heat of the coarse grain (CG) sample is easy to break due to the softening of the CG. With the increase of normal load and sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the HEA samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation. The oxide layer of CG sample has many cracks, and the worn surface also has plastic deformation, which leads to the increase of friction coefficient and specific wear rate and the decrease of wear resistance. Therefore, the fine grain size HEA sample has better wear resistance than the CG sample due to its high surface strength.Keywords: high entropy alloy, grain size, tribological behavior, wear mechanism
